summary:
Our idea: Pranavyom Zero-Gram Health Check turns the tablet astronauts already carry into a clinical decisionsupport sensor. It compares each astronaut to their personal statistical baseline, fuses multi-system vitals with cabin
air sensors, warns them early, and guides action without waiting for Earth.
The problem, in simple words: On long missions to the Moon or Mars, the astronaut's body and mind change:
• Radiation: Raises cancer risk and can affect the brain and central nervous system.
• Microgravity, Bone & Muscle Loss: Weakens hip/spine bones (~1–1.5% loss/month), postural muscles, and the
heart, while pushing fluid toward the head (SANS).
• Nutrition & Hydration Deficit: Spaceflight appetite suppression, inadequate calories/protein, and low fluid
intake accelerate bone/muscle loss and kidney stone formation.
• Hypoxia & Cabin Air: Low cabin oxygen or elevated CO₂ triggers headaches, cognitive slowing, and hypoxia risk.
• Isolation & Confined Cabin: Causes circadian disruption, poor sleep, stress, low mood, and crew conflict.
• Immune Suppression: Weakens immunity, allowing dormant viruses (like cold sores or shingles) to reactivate.
• Communication Latency: On Mars, a message to Earth takes 4 to 24 minutes one way. Astronauts cannot wait
for a flight surgeon—they must spot trends early and act autonomously.
details:
PRANAVYOM ZERO-GRAM – Team Vyro

Live link: 1. NASA Human Research Program – Five Hazards of Human Spaceflight

https://www.nasa.gov/hrp/hazards

2. NASA – Five Hazards of Human Spaceflight (education page)

https://www.nasa.gov/stem-content/five-hazards-of-human-spaceflight/

3. NASA OCHMO – Radiation Protection Technical Brief (600 mSv career limit, NASA-STD-3001)

https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2023/03/radiation-protection-technical-brief-ochmo.pdf

4. NASA Technical Reports Server – The Headache of Carbon Dioxide Exposures (CO2 pockets)

https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20070017835

5. NASA Technical Reports Server – CO2 on the International Space Station: An Operations Update

https://ntrs.nasa.gov/archive/nasa/casi.ntrs.nasa.gov/20150019624.pdf

WHAT IT IS

A health-monitoring web app for astronauts on long missions such as a 450-day Mars trip. Each day the astronaut does a 3–4 minute check-in on a tablet. The app compares the results with that astronaut's own normal values, shows 7 body systems as Green, Yellow or Red, and explains in plain words what to do, without waiting for doctors on Earth, who can be up to 22 minutes away by radio.

PROBLEM IT SOLVES

Long missions expose astronauts to radiation, isolation, altered gravity and a closed environment, causing immune changes, bone loss, heart problems and behavioural issues. Astronauts must detect these themselves.

- Radiation: dosimeter tracking dose rate, daily dose and career dose

- Isolation / behavioural health: mood, stress, energy, sleep, journal, anonymous buddy flag

- Altered gravity: grip steadiness, exercise (ARED) log, eye tests for SANS, hydration, blood-clot (VTE) monitor

- Heart: heart rate, blood oxygen, chest-pain emergency flag

- Immune: symptom log, anaemia blood test every 30 days

- Closed environment: cabin CO2, O2, pressure, temperature, humidity

HOW IT WORKS

1. Sign in by selecting a crew member (CREW-01 to CREW-16).

2. Six daily tests: reaction tap (brain speed), Amsler grid and contrast (eyes/SANS), spatial memory (thinking), grip hold and ARED (muscle and bone), hydration (kidney-stone risk), mood and symptoms (behavioural health).

3. Scoring: each value becomes a Z-score = (today's value − personal average) ÷ personal spread. Green below 1.5σ, Yellow 1.5σ–2.5σ, Red above 2.5σ, plus fixed safety limits (e.g. SpO2 below 92%). The 7 systems are weighted into a 0–100 health score (Heart 20%, Radiation 20%, Mind 15%, Eyes 15%, Immune 10%, Sleep 10%, Bones 10%). Any Yellow caps the score at 89 and any Red caps it at 49, so one serious problem is never hidden.

4. Action Center: simple steps first, then approved medicines with safety checks, then when to call the Medical Officer.

5. Modules: Health Trends (30-day graphs), Cabin Sensors, Smart Pharmacy (15 medicines, radiation-adjusted expiry, allergy and interaction checks), Blood Tests (every 30 days with spoken reminder), VTE Monitor (every 15 days with emergency flag), Crew & Buddy, Reports to Earth (under 1 KB) with Earth-return readiness, daily reminders with an end-of-day buzzer.

6. Privacy: each astronaut sees only their own data. Four officials (Commander, Medical Officer, Communications Specialist, Space Medicine Researcher) can view the whole crew.

BENEFITS

- Crew self-reliance: astronauts can check and act on their own health.

- Early warning: personal baselines detect small changes that general ranges miss.

- Safety first: simple steps before medicines, all checks built in, never a diagnosis.

- Works fully offline; reports are tiny for the slow deep-space link.

- Covers every hazard in the problem statement.

- Protects personal health privacy.

TECHNOLOGY

- Languages: HTML5, CSS3, vanilla JavaScript (no frameworks)

- Charts: inline SVG drawn by our own code

- Sound: Web Audio API (test sounds, buzzer, alarms), Speech Synthesis API (spoken reminders)

- Storage: browser localStorage, saved separately per Crew ID

- Hosting: GitHub Pages

- Tools: VS Code, Live Server, Git and GitHub, Chrome DevTools, Claude (AI coding assistant, disclosed in README)

- Hardware: none required. Runs in any browser on a laptop or tablet. Heart rate, SpO2, CO2 and radiation values are simulated; in a real mission they would come from wearables, a cabin CO2 sensor and a radiation dosimeter.

CREATIVITY

- The tablet screen itself is the medical test – no extra hardware.

- Personal baselines instead of population averages.

- Score caps so a single red flag can never be hidden.

- CO2 spot sensor: in microgravity, exhaled CO2 collects around the face, so it is measured where the astronaut is.

- Medicine expiry adjusted for space radiation.

- Anonymous buddy flag for behavioural health in isolation.

- Earth-return readiness: is the body ready for gravity again?

- VTE emergency triggers a simulated priority transmission to Earth.

- A different sound for each test and a buzzer for missed tasks.

FACTORS CONSIDERED

Communication delay and low bandwidth; safety (no diagnosis, approved medicines only, red status always shared); ease of use (3–4 minutes, plain language, colour plus text); privacy; space-medicine risks (SANS, bone loss, radiation, anaemia, blood clots, CO2, sleep, mood); honesty (fictional data clearly labelled, AI use disclosed).

LIMITATIONS

Prototype only: fictional data, simulated sensors, no real passwords, not clinically validated. It supports decisions and does not replace a doctor.

FUTURE SCOPE

Connect real wearables and cabin sensors, add secure login, and validate thresholds with flight surgeons.
